message.content:
**Most Famous American Composers (by era)**  

| Era | Composer | Notable Works | Why They’re Famous |
|-----|----------|---------------|--------------------|
| **Early 19th century** | **Stephen Foster** (1826–1864) | “Oh! Susanna,” “Camptown Races” | Pioneer of American popular music; his songs became folk standards. |
| **Late 19th century** | **John Philip Sousa** (1854–1932) | “The Stars and Stripes Forever,” “Washington Post March” | “The March King”; his marches defined American patriotic music. |
| **Early 20th century** | **George Gershwin** (1898–1937) | “Rhapsody in Blue,” “An American in Paris” | Blended classical and jazz idioms; helped legitimize jazz in concert halls. |
| | **Aaron Copland** (1900–1990) | “Appalachian Spring,” “Rodeo” | “American Sound”; his music evokes the American landscape and spirit. |
| | **Leonard Bernstein** (1918–1990) | “West Side Story,” “Candide” | Broadway genius; bridged classical, jazz, and musical theater. |
| | **Duke Ellington** (1899–1974) | “Mood Indigo,” “It Don’t Mean a Thing” | Jazz icon; his compositions shaped the big‑band era. |
| | **Charles Ives** (1874–1954) | “The Unanswered Question,” “The Swimmer” | Experimental modernist; integrated American vernacular into classical forms. |
| **Mid‑20th century** | **Philip Glass** (born 1937) | “Glassworks,” “Einstein on the Beach” | Minimalist pioneer; his repetitive structures influenced film and contemporary music. |
| | **John Adams** (born 1947) | “Nixon in China,” “Short Ride in a Fast Machine” | Post‑minimalist; his works are widely performed and recorded. |
| | **Leonard Bernstein** (again) | “West Side Story” (1957) | Continues to be a staple of American musical theater. |
| **Late 20th century** | **John Williams** (born 1942) | “Star Wars,” “Jurassic Park” | Film composer whose themes are instantly recognizable worldwide. |
| | **Kurt Weill** (1900–1950) | “The Threepenny Opera,” “Mahagonny” | German-born but influential in American musical theater and film. |
| **21st century** | **John Adams** (again) | “The Death of Klinghoffer” (1991) | Continues to shape contemporary classical music. |
| | **Jennifer Higdon** (born 1962) | “Blue Cathedral,” “Concerto for Violin and Orchestra” | Pulitzer Prize winner; her music is widely performed. |
| | **Eric Whitacre** (born 1970) | “Lux Aurumque,” “Sleep” | Contemporary choral composer; his works are popular in both concert and community settings. |

**Why These Names Stand Out**

- **Cultural Impact**: Their music has become part of the American cultural fabric—marches, jazz standards, Broadway hits, and film scores.
- **Innovation**: Many pushed musical boundaries—Copland’s “American Sound,” Ives’ experimentalism, Glass’s minimalism.
- **Recognition**: They have received major awards (Pulitzer, Grammy, Academy Awards) and their works are performed worldwide.

These composers represent a broad spectrum of American musical history, from early folk and patriotic tunes to modern film scores and contemporary classical music.
